Testosterone isn’t only a male hormone. It is the most biologically active hormone in women.

Women have testosterone receptors in every cell of their body. Testosterone affects their brain, bones, muscles, mood, energy, memory and libido. When women are younger, their testosterone levels are higher than their estradiol levels.

Testosterone levels usually start to fall from the late 20s and early 30s and many women then notice symptoms without knowing why. They often feel exhausted, lose their motivation, struggle to concentrate, have aching muscles and joints, or lose interest in sex. Too often each symptom is treated separately, so many women are misdiagnosed with depression, personality disorders, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, when the cause underneath is never looked at.

Bioidentical testosterone, usually prescribed as a cream or gel, can be taken with HRT or on its own and it shouldn’t be so hard for women to access. There are so many unfounded fears and reservations of prescribing testosterone which are harming women. Leaving symptoms untreated has real consequences and this need to change.

If you’ve listened to this week’s episode of drlouisenewsonpodcast with researcher Aini Kamal, you’ll have heard me talk about when I asked a panel at a conference about why raised FSH levels are in the guidelines to diagnose POI (menopause in women under 40) when there is no good quality evidence for this. Here is the clip of their response to my question.

The panel couldn’t give any good evidence. Prof Martha Hickey, who was the key topic advisor for the revised NICE menopause guidelines that state this, challenged me on how I make a diagnosis of menopause in young women, and seemed concerned about prescribing safe hormone treatments to women with symptoms. They were not aware that antipsychotic drugs such as quetiapine can reduce FSH levels and lead to a chemical menopause occurring. 

Since then, my research team and I have reviewed the FSH levels of 61 women diagnosed with POI in my newson.health clinic, and the majority had low FSH levels. They wouldn’t have met the guideline criteria, yet they had clear symptoms of POI and responded well to being prescribed bioidentical hormone treatments.

This is important because when women are dismissed for having a normal or low FSH, they are denied hormone treatments that would improve both their symptoms and their long-term health. Guidelines should be evidence based, so when they prevent women being prescribed appropriate treatment we have to question them and make sure they reflect real world evidence.

One of the questions the three of us hear most from women is: “What can I do if I’ve been told no?”

A global survey of more than 3,500 women found over 60% had seen multiple healthcare professionals before getting hormone treatment. One in ten had more than ten GP appointments first. That’s not acceptable.

In my new Substack with jill.chmielewski and Dr Val Pollard, we share practical steps if you’ve been refused and what many clinicians should do differently. I’ve shared a link to the full article in my story.

The “hormones” in contraception are not hormones.

I was chatting with Dr Val Pollard, who I trained with at medical school and who now works with me at newson.health, and we both admitted that for many years we prescribed contraception wrongly believing we were prescribing hormones, and we also thought that the progesterone-only pill was simply progesterone. It isn’t. 

Contraceptives contain synthetic progestogens and, in the combined pill, ethinylestradiol, and no cell in the human body produces progestogens or ethinylestradiol. They have completely different chemical structures to our own hormones and the natural, bioidentical hormone treatments we prescribe now, and these synthetic hormones are associated with risks, including risk of heart disease, clots and cancer. 

That’s why the blanket term HRT is so unhelpful, because it groups very different treatments together as though they’re the same. 

Language matters in medicine and women deserve to know exactly what they are being prescribed so they can make an informed choice and be educated about risks of each treatment.

Why are only around 5% of menopausal women prescribed HRT?

This week on my drlouisenewsonpodcast, Dr Jerrold Weinberg menopausemended, an obstetrician and gynaecologist who has practised medicine for 50 years, explained how we got here. When a woman stops making estradiol, the simple answer is to replace it, yet there are still unfounded fears about HRT. The first hormone treatments were made from pregnant mares' urine (Premarin) and the synthetic progestogen medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera) which are associated with small risks. However, these are very different to the bioidentical hormone treatments we prescribe now which are not associated with these risks. However, there are a whole generation of doctors who have not been trained to prescribe hormone treatments.

The bioidentical hormone treatments, progesterone, estradiol and testosterone, which we prescribe now are the same structure as the hormones our bodies make and are therefore very different from the older types of HRT. Women who are prescribed the right dose and type of bioidentical hormone treatments often them feel like themselves again, as well as having better future health.

Every woman struggling with symptoms of hormonal changes, at any age, deserves the chance to make an informed choice about being prescribed hormone treatments.

No one considered hormone treatments then and she was told the risks were too high. Now she doesn’t want to take bisphosphonates because she’s read about their risks, yet she’s been told she has to. 

Her GP documented what he thought the risks of HRT are, including cardiovascular disease, stroke and breast cancer, but not that those risks relate to synthetic hormones rather than the body identical hormones we prescribe now. Estradiol, progesterone and testosterone work physiologically on bone, helping osteoblasts build it and reducing the osteoclasts that break it down. Women deserve a choice and the best evidence. I listened to this guardianscience  podcast today about perimenopause.

There was discussion here that many women’s symptoms could be due to “stress” and women were encouraged to change their lifestyle to improve symptoms such as increase exercise. 

They also spoke about women being prescribed “hormonal” contraception and wait until they are 50 before considering taking HRT. 

Hormone levels start to fluctuate and fall long before menopause, and those changes affect the brain, bones, heart and every other system in the body, causing many symptoms including mood changes and anxiety - important to consider rather than giving women the label of “stress”. 

We should also have healthy lifestyles but they won’t replace hormones that are low.

Contraception contains synthetic hormones, which actually can block the action of your own hormones (progesterone, estradiol and testosterone) and are associated with risks of clot, heart disease, stroke and cancers, unlike bioidentical hormone treatments. 

If the underlying cause of a woman’s symptoms is low hormones, we should be replacing them with the right dose and type of hormone treatment. 

Every woman deserves accurate information so she can make her own choice about taking hormone treatments. 

Women deserve to feel better and live healthier lives by having better access to bioidentical hormone treatments - progesterone, estradiol and testosterone - and also to vaginal hormones.

Does menopause speed up ageing and can estrogen slow it down?

nikolinalauc, CEO of glycanage, joined me on my drlouisenewsonpodcast to explain what her research shows about inflammation, ageing and the menopause transition.

Before menopause, women are in a way protected against low-grade inflammation, and when you compare their immune systems with men's, they look much younger. Nikolina's research with Professor Tim Spector found that from perimenopause to menopause, this marker of immune ageing changes twice as fast as at any other time in a woman's life, which helps explain why heart disease and diabetes so often appear after menopause. Studies have shown that estrogen can prevent this acceleration, and in a group of women from my newson.health clinic, inflammation fell with HRT.

When a recent review of UK Biobank data identified 14 drugs with the potential to extend life, four of them were estrogens, and yet the longevity world is focused on new drugs because estrogen is generic. Many diseases of ageing are inflammatory, and while we can't always prevent them, we may be able to delay them, so women can stay healthier for longer.

SNL’s “Sister” sketch hit so hard because it isn’t really satire; it’s the default long-term care plan in this country, and it runs on women’s unpaid time.

Of the 63 million Americans providing family care right now, 61 percent are women, and the average caregiver is 51: right in the window of menopause (AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, Caregiving in the U.S. 2025). In dementia care, more than one in three caregivers is a daughter (Alzheimer’s Association, 2025).

The money shows it most clearly. A MetLife analysis of Health and Retirement Study data (2011) put the average lifetime loss for a woman caring for an aging parent at $324,044 in wages, Social Security, and pension, compared with $283,716 for men. Caregivers spend an average of $7,242 a year out of pocket, about 26 percent of their income (AARP, 2021), and in 2025 nearly half reported a major financial hit like taking on debt, stopping savings, or not being able to afford food.

Your body keeps a ledger too. In a six-year study published in PNAS in 2003, Janice Kiecolt-Glaser’s team found that IL-6, an inflammatory marker linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and frailty, rose about four times faster in people caring for a spouse with dementia, and the rise didn’t slow even years after caregiving ended. That study looked at spouses; we don’t have the same data on midlife daughters caring for parents, and that’s a gap worth funding.

Now, this doesn’t mean caregiving itself will make you sick. The research points to strain: long hours, no help, no relief.

The system’s backup plan is your sister. Women deserve a real one. Paid family leave, respite care, and a clinician who asks who’s taking care of you. Send this to your sibling (you know which one).

“How long should I stay on HRT?” is a question I get all the time. Many women worry if it’s even worth starting if they might have to stop soon after.

The truth is, there’s no “hard and fast” rule that you must stop after five years. It’s a very individual decision based on your own health.

Here is what we consider:

👉 Individual Assessment: We regularly weigh up if the benefits of staying on HRT outweigh any risks for you personally.

👉 Modern Safety: Using newer, body-identical HRT is a much safer option.

👉 Protective Benefits: When started during perimenopause or early menopause, HRT protects your bones and likely your heart and blood vessels too.

👉 Feeling Better: Most importantly, it helps you feel like yourself again.

The best approach is to have regular chats with your doctor to stay up to date with the latest guidance and ensure the best outcome for you.

Is there a link between HRT and Alzheimer’s? It’s a question I hear often.

While we are still learning, here is what the current data shows:

👉 Women make up two-thirds of Alzheimer’s cases.

👉 Oestrogen is very active in our brains.

👉 Brain imaging shows changes during menopause long before memory shifts occur.

👉 Longer lifetime exposure to oestrogen is likely protective.

👉 Early or surgical menopause without replacement may increase risk.

Deciding on HRT is about looking at the full picture of your individual health and benefits.

October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and this time last year I was starting my own breast cancer treatment. With follow-up scans and appointments this month, being back in those waiting rooms and waiting for answers has brought so much of that fear and health anxiety back.

What I hadn’t understood until I went through it myself was how difficult it can feel to have reminders everywhere. You can be having a lovely moment with your children, shopping or scrolling, and something takes you straight back to a hospital room or a fear you’d put to one side for a wee while.

I know how much love and good intention goes into this month. I’m grateful for the awareness, fundraising and conversations that encourage women to get checked. I’ve spent years having those conversations myself and I know how much they matter. I’m also discovering how hard it can be when you’re finding your feet following a diagnosis and there’s very little space to get away from it.

I also feel like I should be doing more. I have a platform, I’m a doctor, and I want to be shouting about checking your breasts and getting any changes checked, as I always have done. I will continue to do that because it matters so much to me. It’s just that right now, gosh, it feels so close to the bone, and somehow I find myself needing a bit of space from the very thing I want to help others understand.

Some of you might feel it too, whether you’re waiting for answers, going through treatment, living with breast cancer, finding your way through life afterwards or have lost someone to breast cancer. You can appreciate everything this month is trying to do and still find the reminders difficult.

If you need to scroll past, mute things or spend less time online, you’re allowed to. You don’t have to share your story or get involved just because it’s October.

there was a time when i genuinely wanted to crawl out of my own skin.

the anxiety was so unbearable that i literally wanted to be outside of my own body.

i was 37 when the anxiety and panic attacks began.

the smallest thing would set me off.

my husband could brake hard in traffic and i’d be beside myself. heart racing, body flooded with panic. it could take me 15 minutes to calm down.

i’d watch my children at their swimming lessons and imagine them drowning.

the phone would ring and i’d assume the worst.

someone’s hurt. someone’s ill.

i was catastrophising everything.

and the worst part? i knew it was irrational.

knowing that didn’t stop it.

it was like my brain couldn’t tell the difference between real danger and something that might happen. and my body reacted to both as though my life depended on it.

there were moments when i genuinely felt like something in my brain was going to snap.

writing this now, it sounds dramatic. but at the time, i felt like i was drowning in it.

and i had no idea perimenopause could be playing a part.

nobody had explained that oestrogen doesn’t just influence your periods. it also interacts with brain systems involved in mood, anxiety and our response to stress.

as oestrogen fluctuates in perimenopause, some women become more vulnerable to anxiety and panic. anxiety can have other causes, too, so new or severe symptoms deserve assessment.

but here’s what i wish i’d understood.

when your brain is constantly anticipating danger, you can start to lose trust in your own mind.

you question whether you’re coping, or whether this is just who you’ve become.

i wasn’t just frightened of what might happen to the people i loved.

i was frightened of what was happening inside my own head.

i spent so long wondering what was wrong with me, when what i really needed was to understand what was happening to me.

if this sounds familiar, please know there’s so much you can do to support yourself. and that’s exactly what i create content about.

follow whatthemenopause to understand what’s happening in your body and what you can do to feel like yourself again.

What if the story you’re telling yourself about menopause is quietly shaping how you experience it?

“I’m getting old.”

“I’ve let myself go.”

“My body doesn’t work anymore.”

“Maybe this is just who I am now.”

Here’s what I want you to understand.

Your brain is not a passive observer of your life.

Your expectations influence what you pay attention to, how you interpret experiences, and what you remember.

Psychologists call some of these processes selective attention and confirmation bias.

And when you’ve spent years telling yourself you’re failing, it’s easy to turn every disappointing weigh-in, missed workout or difficult day into another piece of evidence against yourself.

While overlooking the progress you’re making.

But this goes so much deeper than your weight.

What happens when you start believing menopause is the beginning of your decline?

That your energy will never return.

That you’re not as capable as you used to be.

That your best years are behind you.

You may start lowering your expectations.

Stop pursuing the things you want.

Stop believing you can feel phenomenal again.

And that’s the part I want to challenge.

Because your hormonal changes are REAL.

Your symptoms are REAL.

And none of this means you can simply think your way out of perimenopause.

But your beliefs can influence how you respond to what you’re experiencing.

And that’s something you can begin to change.

Start noticing what’s working.

Look for evidence of the promises you’re keeping.

Approach setbacks with curiosity instead of self-criticism.

And stop treating every difficult moment as proof that you’re failing.

Menopause is not the beginning of the end.

You have an extraordinary amount of life left to live.

And I want you going ALL IN on who you’re becoming.

Not someday.

NOW.

Before your feet hit the floor in the morning, gently wake up your joints.

Joints feel stiff in the morning because they’ve had relatively little movement overnight. Joint fluid distribution,  surrounding tissues and underlying conditions like osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis or menopause can all contribute.

Gentle movement can restore mobility, warm up the muscles and reduce the feeling of stiffness.

Video sped up. Move slowly and mindfully: 
1) Spread the fingers and rotate hands and feet five times in one direction and five times in the other direction

2) hug one knee to chest and hold for five breaths then hug the other knee

3) Placing feet wider than hips, drop both of knees  to one side then to the other side. 

4) Give yourself a full body stretch by reaching with the heels in one direction and the fingertips in the other

5) slowly make your way to a comfortable seated position and twist to one side stay there for five breaths then twist to the other side

6) seated cat cows mobilise the spine. Place your hands on your knees, inhale to lift the chest and look up at the ceiling then exhale rounding the spine and bringing your chin towards your chest 5 times.

One of the most overlooked effects of perimenopause is a drop in gut microbial diversity. Emerging research shows that the gut microbiome of postmenopausal women is less diverse and metabolically different from that of premenopausal women, largely due to the decline in estrogen and progesterone in late perimenopause. These hormone changes alter the gut’s “estrobolome,” the collection of bacteria involved in estrogen metabolism.

Lower diversity matters because the microbiome plays a role in so many things, from metabolic health and inflammation to body composition, bone density, and brain function. Studies show menopause-related microbiome changes are associated with higher waist circumference, blood pressure, and cardiometabolic risk markers.

This is one reason many women notice shifts in weight, energy, digestion, and mood during the menopause transition.

In my last newsletter, I wrote about perimenopause and menopause hormone therapy: how to spot the signs of perimenopause, how to find the right healthcare provider, and what to expect when you start MHT. Today, I’m picking up where I left off with the part I feel most strongly about: what active women should know and consider about MHT.

MHT is a tool, and a good one, but—as with so many things—lifestyle can be just as powerful (if not more so for some) and needs to be considered too. 

As I mentioned in Part 1, most experts now use the term MHT rather than HRT, because the goal isn’t to “replace” the hormones you once had. That distinction is the root of a lot of confusion.

The hormones in MHT don’t behave exactly like the ones your ovaries made. Treatment doses aim for a steady, low physiological level, not the higher pulses and rhythms of your natural cycle, and your body responds differently to them. So replacing some estrogen doesn’t mean restoring everything estrogen once did. 

How you take estradiol matters:

- Pills (oral) are processed by the liver before reaching the rest of the body, so much of the estradiol is converted to estrone, a weaker estrogen. The liver also makes more clotting proteins, which slightly raises the risk of blood clots. 

- Patches and gels (transdermal) absorb through the skin straight into the bloodstream, keeping a more natural balance of estrogens with little effect on the liver. 

MHT can ease menopausal symptoms and protect tissues like bone and the vaginal and urinary tract, but it isn’t a like-for-like replacement.

That’s why the research shows MHT is first and foremost a tool for symptom relief, with bone protection as its clearest long-term benefit. The literature doesn’t show it builds muscle, drives fat loss, or prevents heart disease (one major trial suggests it may slow early arterial changes when started soon after menopause, but that’s not the same as prevention). This is where the lifestyle levers like sleep, exercise, and nutrition really come to the fore.

For decades, aerobic exercise was regarded as the primary form of exercise you should do for cardiovascular and other health benefits. Now, finally, the new American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement in Circulation makes the argument that, “Resistance training not only can improve or maintain muscle mass and strength, but also has favorable physiological and clinical effects on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.”

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is one of the topics I’m asked about most, and the conversation around it has changed dramatically over the years. For two decades after the 2002 Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study, women were told hormones were dangerous (which was largely a fault of media misinterpreting the design and results of the study). Now the pendulum has swung hard the other way, and if you believe everything you read on the internet you’d think every woman needs MHT, for life, or her health will fall apart.

The truth sits somewhere in the middle. MHT is a genuinely useful tool, and for many women it can be life-changing. But it isn’t a cure-all, and it doesn’t replace the lifestyle foundations that drive your health through midlife and beyond.

There’s so much to cover on this topic that I’ve split it into two parts. This week, we’ll cover recognizing the signs, finding the right provider, testing, and what to expect when you start. In my next newsletter on November 2, we’ll cover what MHT does (and doesn’t do) for your body, the testosterone question, non-hormonal options, and how long to stay on it.

An important note before we dive in: MHT is often also referred to as HRT (hormone replacement therapy) or simply HT (hormone therapy). They all describe the same treatment, but most experts now prefer MHT, because the goal isn’t to "replace" the hormones you previously had. It’s to ease symptoms and protect your health through this stage of life.

Yet women are disproportionately affected by cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease. Alzheimer’s is a brain condition that slowly damages memory, thinking, learning, and organizational skills. It is an abnormal buildup of amyloid and tau proteins that prevent neurons from working as they should.

There is not enough attention drawn to the fact that nearly two-thirds of Alzheimer’s cases are women, and women have a greater lifetime risk of developing the disease than men (the risk is 1 in 5 for women versus 1 in 10 for men). Women are often diagnosed later than men because the key memory tests doctors use rely on verbal skills—and women tend to do better on those, even in the early stages of decline. As a result, problems can be missed at first. But once symptoms do show up, women often decline more quickly, likely because they have a higher buildup of harmful tau proteins in the brain. This may be linked to differences in how women’s brains naturally clear out damaged cells and waste.

Although there is clearly a knowledge gap (as there is with so much of the health and fitness data women rely on), we can begin tracing the answers back to female biology, hormones, and how our brains respond to stress, inflammation, and aging across the lifespan. What changed?

I learned how pain *actually* works.

All pain is ultimately experienced through the brain. And some of the same brain networks involved in physical pain are also involved in stress, fear and emotional distress. When we’re chronically stressed or feel unsafe, the brain can become more protective and amplify pain.

Pain does not always equal damage. And a structural finding does not automatically mean that finding is why you hurt.

We also know that structural “abnormalities”—disc degeneration, bulging discs, arthritis, labral tears, tendon changes and more—are often found in people who have NO pain.

The finding can be real.
The pain can be real.
And the finding still may not explain the pain.

Chronic pain is far more complex than “something hurts, therefore something must be damaged and need fixing.”

For years, I believed my feet were the problem.

Then I learned the neuroscience of pain and began teaching my brain and nervous system that my body wasn’t broken and movement was safe.

Eventually, the pain disappeared.

No surgery.
No orthotics.
No pain.

8 pain-free years later, man am I glad I learned how pain actually works before I let someone reconstruct both of my ankles. 😵‍💫

If you live with chronic pain, please learn the neuroscience of pain.

It might just change your life too.

If you’re taking a GLP-1 or helping someone who is, here are three important things to know:

1. When you lose weight on these medications, you lose both muscle and fat. That’s why eating enough protein and doing resistance training are still important, even if your appetite goes down. This helps make sure most of the weight you lose is fat, and you keep the muscle you need for long-term health.

2. These medications can lower bone density over time, and it’s something people often miss.

3. GLP-1s slow down how quickly your stomach empties, so nausea and constipation are common side effects. These usually get better as your body adjusts, but it’s still important to manage them.

The TRIUMPH-1 phase 3 trial of retatrutide (published in the NEJM) involved 2,339 adults with obesity. They were randomly assigned to receive 4 mg, 9 mg, 12 mg of the drug or placebo for 80 weeks. The mean starting BMI was 40.

Participants on the 12mg dose lost an average of 28.3% body weight. When you look at the whole cohort, the average weight loss was 25%. Placebo group lost 2.2%. At the highest dose 5.3% of people either reduced or stopped treatment as their weight loss was deemed to be too much or sufficient. Discontinuation due to side effects was 11.3% at 12mg and 4.9% on placebo.

With the amount of weight loss we’re talking about, I’m interested in what sort of tissue was actually lost, but the paper gives us no body composition data. The earlier phase 2 DEXA data in the T2D population showed that 30-40% of the weight lost was lean tissue which is in keeping with what you’d expect from other anti-obesity meds. As the DXA lean soft tissue figure encompasses more than just skeletal muscle I’d like to see skeletal muscle measured directly. Training and protein are obviously the most important things to protect muscle.

Retatrutide is still under investigation and has not been approved by the FDA.

As you get older the quality of your protein intake becomes a non-negotiable factor in the defence of skeletal muscle tissue.

Animal proteins provide a potent, highly bioavailable profile of the essential amino acids required for muscle protein synthesis. Most plant proteins fall short of this in terms of both concentration and essential amino acid profile (i.e. they are deficient in one or more of the essential amino acids) and as such are unable to adequately stimulate muscle adaptation. This is the very basis of the FAO’s digestibility coefficient for the essential amino acids.

Plant protein can certainly be part of the picture once you’ve established your daily intake with high quality protein. The marginal benefit of protein quality falls away once you’ve hit your minimum of 1.6g per kg of body weight. Some plant sources (soy in particular) are fairly good in terms of amino acid profile, the majority however are not very good for driving muscle protein synthesis.

References:

FAO. 2013. Dietary protein quality evaluation in human nutrition. Report of an FAO Expert Consultation. PMID: 26369006.

Hevia-Larraín V et al. 2021. High-protein plant-based diet versus a protein-matched omnivorous diet to support resistance training adaptations: a comparison between habitual vegans and omnivores. PMID: 33599941.

Monteyne AJ et al. 2023. Vegan and omnivorous high protein diets support comparable daily myofibrillar protein synthesis rates and skeletal muscle hypertrophy in young adults. PMID: 36822394.

Morton RW et al. 2018. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. PMID: 28698222.

Two recent clinical trials have looked at the effect of removing animal protein from the diet on muscle mass in older people.

In the first study, adults over 65 on a vegan diet for 12 weeks lost about 5% of thigh muscle volume, protein intake dropping to 0.8g/kg/day. Those on the vegan diet who also did strength training lost muscle too, just about half as much.

In the second study, adults over 55 who were doing resistance training three times a week and following mostly vegetarian diets saw an increase in muscle mass. Those who were eating some meat in their diet gained more muscle in their arms and legs and had a higher protein intake.

You can build muscle on a predominantly plant-based diet as long as your total protein intake is adequate and includes sources that provide all the essential amino acids required for muscle maintenance.
